products.title: Annie's Potteries x Bird Collective Hand Made Pigeon Mug
products.body:
We collaborated with Brooklyn ceramicist Annie Wong of Annie’s Potteries to create these one-of-a-kind, handmade mugs. Featuring pigeons alongside familiar city icons, each piece is a little celebration of our favorite urban bird and the cities they call home.

Because each mug is made entirely by hand, no two are exactly alike. Variations in the design pattern and imperfections in the clay, glaze, shape, and finish are a natural part of the handmade process and make each piece uniquely its own.

Handmade pottery for your everyday coffee, tea, or whatever you’re sipping. Comes with free stickers inside!

products.title: Pigeon Sidewalk Tee
products.body: In a city, theres no more iconic sound than the "Coo, roo-c'too-coo" of a flock of pigeons on the sidewalk. This graphic tee celebrates our familiar, often misunderstood neighbors and the sights and sounds they bring to city streets.

products.title: Pigeon Flight Cropped Tee
products.body: Today, pigeons in flight, like the one on this cropped tee, are a familiar sight across North American cities. But they haven't always just flown across city skies. Rock Pigeons carried messages for the U.S. Army Signal Corps during World Wars I and II, saving lives and providing vital strategic information with their flights.

products.title: Pigeon Barb Hat
products.body: This dad hat celebrates the tenacity of pigeons, who have proven they can survive just about anything, from winter to traffic to the side-eye from NYC commuters.

products.title: Pigeon Sticker
products.body: The Rock Pigeon on this sticker is shown in its common "blue-bar" form, with bluish-gray plumage, two black wing bands, and a black-tipped tail. Pigeons come in many different shades and patterns, which you can spot in flocks just about anywhere.

products.title: Pigeon Sidewalk Hat
products.body: Rock Pigeons flock about on this flat brim cap, in groups that typically number around 50 but can reach upwards of 500 birds!  Resilient, social, and often misunderstood, these city dwellers have lived alongside us for thousands of years.

products.title: Pigeon Nest Tie Dye Tee
products.body: This tie dye celebrates the Rock Pigeon, a staple of urban areas across North America. In the wild, these birds nest on cliffs and rocky ledges across Europe, North Africa, and Asia, but the pigeons brought to North America in the early 17th century have since taken to roosting on the ledges and rooftops of human cities.

products.title: Pigeon Flight Tie Dye Tee
products.body: Pigeons in flight, such as the one on this tie dye tee, use many different methods to navigate. They can sense the Earth’s magnetic field, rely on visual landmarks, and even use the sun as a compass to find their way home. Just one of the many reasons these highly intelligent birds deserve a little more appreciation.

products.title: Pigeon Sweatpants

products.title: Pigeon Collage Tee

This tee celebrates these highly intelligent, often misunderstood birds with a collage honoring the many sides of our longtime city neighbors.

products.title: Pigeon Sidewalk Tank
products.body: Pigeons have lived alongside humans for more than 5,000 years, first as cherished companions and domesticated birds, and today as familiar city neighbors. This muscle tee celebrates the resilient flocks that still gather on the sidewalks of New York City.

products.title: Pigeon Flight Sweatshirt

products.title: Pigeon Nest Long Sleeve Tee
products.body: This comfy black long sleeve tee celebrates a common sight in cities around the world, the Rock Pigeon. Introduced to North America from Europe in the early 1600s, these birds originally roosted in crevices, caves, and cliffsides in the wild. Today, they’ve adapted to city life, making their homes on buildings and window ledges alongside us.

products.title: Pigeon Dad Hat
products.body: Resilient, intelligent, and deeply connected to humans for thousands of years, pigeons have earned their place in our cities and our hearts. Pigeons have such a long history with humans, dating back to Egypt and even Mesopotamia, that it's impossible to tell what their original range was.

products.title: Greater White-fronted Goose Patch
products.body:
#87 Greater White-fronted Goose

A brown-gray goose with bright orange legs and a pinkish bill ringed with white, the Greater White-fronted is a serious traveler. These geese breed on Arctic tundra across the Northern Hemisphere, and migrate south to fields and wetlands in North America, Europe, and Asia. Outside of the breeding season, they form large flocks and their laughter-like calls—hence the nickname of Laughing Goose—can be heard from loose lines passing overhead.

products.title: Rock Pigeon Patch
products.body:
#86 Rock Pigeon

Walk around any city and you will see Rock Pigeons. They’re in streets and squares, living off discarded food and nesting on buildings and window ledges, under train stations and bridges. Domesticated more than 5,000 years ago, they’ve traveled with us around the world, raised for food and trained for homing, racing, and carrying messages. They were introduced to North America from Europe in the early 1600s. Though the typical city pigeon is blue-gray with two dark wingbars, they come in several other colors and patterns.

#85 Barn Swallow Patch

Agile, graceful flyers, Barn Swallows skim low over open water and open fields in search of flying insect prey. They are steely blue above and rust-colored below, and their forked tails set them apart from all other North American swallows. They breed throughout the Northern Hemisphere and spend winters in much of the Southern Hemisphere. They often build their cup-shaped mud nests on human-made structures, such as bridges and houses.

Large, long-legged, and dazzlingly white, the Great Egret is a showstopper. In the breeding season, showy plumes—called aigrettes—fan from its back, and its lores (between bill and eye) turn neon green. Once hunted nearly to extinction for these plumes to adorn women’s hats, the Great Egret helped spark the modern conservation movement and some of the first laws protecting birds. Today, it is common in wetlands across the globe.

The aptly named Roseate Spoonbill is a large, bright pink wading bird with a partly bald head and a long bill that widens at the tip. It forages in groups in shallow fresh and saltwater, sweeping up crustaceans and fish. Carotenoid pigments in its prey give it its pink color. One of six spoonbill species worldwide, it’s the only one found in the Western Hemisphere, ranging from the southeastern U.S. to South America.

products.title: Blackburnian Warbler Patch
products.body:
#82 Blackburnian Warbler

With its flame-orange face and throat, the Blackburnian Warbler is a star of spring migration in the eastern U.S. A long-distance migrant, it breeds in northern spruce forests, where it sings from treetops, and winters in the Andes, where it’s common in open forests and shade coffee plantations. These birds are forest-canopy specialists, so it’s best to remember their song: a thin, fast sequence that rises to an ear-splitting pitch.

This patch is inspired by the Black Swamp Bird Observatory in northwest Ohio, a key migration area for Blackburnian Warblers.

The breeding adults are distinctive, with sleek black heads, white eye crescents, and red bills. They can be found looking for handouts on beaches, docks, and parking lots, from the Northeast in the summer to the Gulf of Mexico all year round.

products.title: Feather Friendly Black Triple Roll
products.body:
Start protecting your windows and the birds around your home with the Feather Friendly Black Triple Roll. Designed for residential glass surfaces like windows, patio doors, and clear panels, these visual markers help birds recognize barriers they might otherwise fly into.

This DIY kit includes three roll of high-contrast black markers spaced for optimal visibility to birds, two paper measuring tapes, a squeegee, clear installation instructions, and a bird-safe sticker — everything you need to start protecting your winged visitors quickly and confidently.

Applied to the exterior surface of your glass, black markers are better for applications where birds can see through the glass and attempt to fly to whatever is beyond, such as glass railings, without significantly impacting your view or natural light. In contrast, white markers break up reflections and make transparent panes visible to birds, which is best for glass that primarily presents a reflection hazard — for example, where birds see reflections of sky or vegetation that could confuse them. This makes black markers more suitable for railings and transparent panels, while white markers are best for building windows.

Easy to install and highly effective, this solution blends practicality with a meaningful purpose: helping reduce bird-glass collisions around your home while keeping your windows looking clean and unobtrusive.

1/4" x 100ft per roll

Featured Components

• Three rolls of Feather Friendly® Small-format DIY black markers
• Two paper measuring tapes
• One squeegee
• One bird-safe sticker

Applied to the exterior surface of your glass, the white markers break up reflections and make transparent panes visible to birds, without significantly impacting your view or natural light. White markers are ideal for glass that primarily presents a reflection hazard — for example, where birds see reflections of sky or vegetation that could confuse them. In contrast, black markers are better for applications where birds can see through the glass and attempt to fly to whatever is beyond, such as glass railings. This makes white markers best for building windows, while black markers are more suitable for railings and transparent panels.

Easy to install and highly effective, this solution blends practicality with a meaningful purpose: helping reduce bird-glass collisions around your home while keeping your windows looking clean and unobtrusive.

products.title: Bird City
products.body:
Bird City: Adventures in New York's Urban Wilds

Written by Ryan Goldberg

For readers of What an Owl Knows and The World Without Us, this infectiously impassioned tour of the five New York City boroughs offers city dwellers and bird lovers everywhere a surprising, delightful new view of the concrete jungle—through its abundant and diverse bird population.

Ryan Goldberg came to birding unexpectedly, but as many first-timers do after seeing their “spark” bird, he fell hard. Enamored with the incredible variety of species that pass through his hometown of New York City, and with the other passionate birders he meets, he embarks on a year of reporting on the natural wonders hiding amidst the skyscrapers. He learns that millions of birds migrate through the city each year—more than four hundred different species have been found in New York, many more than in Yellowstone National Park.
 
Through the four seasons, Goldberg takes readers to all five boroughs, through the city’s most famous parks and landmarks. He pursues rare and common species alike, increasing his count and deepening his understanding of how and why birds make their home in this smoggy, noisy, concrete-coated environment. Along the way, he meets many delightful and idiosyncratic characters, both human and feathered. 
 
Richly textured, informative, and uplifting, Bird City will inspire fast-walking New Yorkers, the ever-growing birding community, and readers everywhere who think of “nature” as just a place to visit on Saturdays to slow down and look around them. There’s a lot more than pigeons in our city skies.

Though a member of the falcon family, the Yellow-headed Caracara behaves more like a vulture, frequently eating carrion on the ground. The species inhabits open country from northern Argentina to Costa Rica, but is slowly expanding its range north due to deforestation in Central America. An omnivorous and opportunistic feeder, it will perch on cattle, capybaras, and tapirs to pick off ticks. Still an “accidental” species in the American Birding Association area, sightings in 2024 in Florida, Texas, and California have drawn hordes of U.S. birders.

With Eric Eaton as your guide, you will circle the globe in search of African Toktokkies and Australian beer bottle beetles, and witness the peculiar spectacle of cricket fighting in Asia. Profiles of influential figures in entomology provide insights into the curious minds that animate this extraordinarily broad field of scientific inquiry, while the book’s portable size makes it the perfect travel companion no matter where your own entomological adventures may lead you.

With captivating illustrations by Amy Jean Porter, Insectpedia is an engaging blend of insect facts and folklore that will inspire anyone who delights in the marvels of nature.

Illustrated by Amy Jean Porter

A delightful illustrated treasury of botanical facts and fancy

Florapedia is an eclectic A–Z compendium of botanical lore. With more than 100 enticing entries—on topics ranging from achlorophyllous plants that use a fungus as an intermediary to obtain nutrients from other plants to zygomorphic flowers that admit only the most select pollinators—this collection is a captivating journey into the realm of botany.

Writing in her incomparably engaging style, Carol Gracie discusses remarkable plants from around the globe, botanical art and artists, early botanical explorers, ethnobotanical uses of plants, botanical classification and terminology, the role of plants in history, and more. She shares illuminating facts about van Gogh’s sunflowers and reveals how a hallucinogenic weed left its enduring mark on the early history of the Jamestown colony. Gracie describes the travels of John and William Bartram—father and son botanists and explorers who roamed widely in early America in search of plants—and delves into the miniature ecosystems entangled in Spanish moss. The book’s convenient size allows for it to be tucked into a pocket or bag, making it the perfect companion on your own travels.

With charming drawings by Amy Jean Porter, Florapedia is the ideal gift book for the plant enthusiast in your life and a rare pleasure for anyone interested in botanical art, history, medicine, or exploration.

products.title: Purple Finch Patch
products.body:
#69 Purple Finch

Small and chunky with big seed-cracking bills, Purple Finches are irregular winter visitors to bird feeders in the U.S. They breed across much of Canada and in northern forests in the U.S., but every few years many head south in the fall to search for food in response to shortages of cone crops. It is the adult male that gives the Purple Finch its common name, though it is really a raspberry red. The females and immatures are a streaky brown.

products.title: Snow Bunting Patch
products.body:
#68 Snow Bunting

Snow Buntings nest in rock cavities of the high Arctic and then turn nomadic, spending winters on beaches, lakeshores, and fields across Canada and the United States. Their rusty coloration in winter blends in with those landscapes. And in the spring, when they return to the cold and treeless tundra, the males will rub their heads and bellies on the snow to wear down the brown feather tips, revealing the white below, which matches the snow.

products.title: Eastern Backyard Birds Ceramic Mug
products.body: Support your local birds! Get excited about the wildlife in your backyard with this fun ceramic mug.

products.title: Surf Scoter Patch
products.body:
#67 Surf Scoter

These velvety sea ducks are bicoastal, spending winters as far south as Baja California and the Gulf Coast, then heading north to breed on freshwater lakes at the edge of the tundra. The males have long candy corn-like bills and white patches on their black domes, giving them the nickname “old skunkhead.” In the winter they mix with Black Scoters and White-winged Scoters, so it pays to know where the white is on each species.

products.title: Support Your Local Birds Ceramic Mug
products.body: Add a touch of charm to your morning routine with our “Support Your Local Birds” mug. This vintage style diner mug features bold, retro-inspired lettering and a whimsical bird illustration, making it the perfect companion for bird lovers and coffee enthusiasts alike. With its comfortable handle and durable design, it’s great for sipping coffee, tea, or hot cocoa while dreaming of your next birdwatching adventure.

products.title: Wandering Albatross Patch
products.body:
#R1 Wandering Albatross

This limited edition patch is part of our Rarities series, and is only available to our Monthly Patch Club subscribers. It's the Patch of the Month for April 2023 only, and then it's gone! 

The Wandering Albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird, measuring up to 11 feet. It nests on islands near the Antarctic Circle and on some in the South Atlantic, and in the nonbreeding season it roams the southern oceans for weeks on the wing, living up to its name. The American Birding Association classifies it as Code-5, meaning it has been recorded five or fewer times in the ABA checklist area: North America north of Mexico and the Hawaiian islands.

products.title: Chimney Swift Patch
products.body:
#66 Chimney Swift

Chimney Swifts spend most of their lives airborne. They can’t perch, so when they do land they cling to the vertical surfaces of chimneys, tree hollows or caves. They’re fixtures of summer evenings in the east, where they fill the skies with their aerial displays and high-pitched chatter. During fall migration, they roost together by the thousands, funneling into chimneys at dusk. If you don’t have a chimney, one thing you can do to help them is to build a swift nesting tower.

products.body: Celebrate nature's cleanup crew in style with this epic Turkey Vulture graphic tee. These important scavengers help keep nature in balance.

products.title: Black Vulture Tee
products.body: This tie-dye tee features an illustration of Black Vultures framed by celestial elements, flames, and bones. These awesome birds play an important role in ecosystems by quickly cleaning up carcasses and controlling the spread of diseases.

products.title: Ruby-throated Hummingbird Corduroy Hat
products.body: This Ruby-throated Hummingbird Corduroy Hat features a mulberry color and an embroidered hummingbird design. Crafted from soft, durable corduroy, this cap offers comfort and style for everyday wear.

products.title: Nikon Prostaff P3 8x42 Binoculars
products.body: Brighten your view with the PROSTAFF P3 8x42 binoculars. Full-size 42mm front objectives gather maximum light for a brighter, clearer view, even as daylight is fading. 8x magnification provides a wide field of view that shows more of the scene and is also easier to hold steady—great for locating wildlife or using the binoculars on the go. A waterproof, fogproof and drop-resistant design means you can take them everywhere, and renowned Nikon optics make every view spectacular. products.title: Turkey Vulture Patch
products.body:
#65 Turkey Vulture

Turkey Vultures are nature’s clean-up crew. Flying low to the ground or above the trees in their characteristic wobble, these scavengers’ sense of smell allows them to find carrion from far away. They have extremely acidic stomachs, and can digest just about anything without getting sick – tuberculosis, botulism, anthrax, rabies – and in turn those diseases don’t spread from the carcasses they pick apart.

products.title: Chickadee Corduroy Dad Hat
products.body:

Made from soft, durable 100% cotton corduroy, this hat offers comfort you can feel and quality that lasts, whether you’re out exploring, birding in the woods, or running errands around town. The tonal embroidered chickadee on the front celebrates one of North America’s most beloved backyard birds, adding nature-inspired charm to a classic silhouette. 

The unstructured six-panel crown and flat bill give the hat a relaxed, timeless look that pairs easily with outdoor gear or casual outfits. An adjustable fabric strap with a metal clasp ensures a comfortable, customizable fit for most head sizes. 

Versatile and fun, the Chickadee Corduroy Hat makes a great gift for fellow bird lovers or a standout staple in your own wardrobe. Whether you’re heading out on a hike or adding a touch of everyday style, this hat brings a bit of avian personality wherever you go.

products.title: Birds of Eastern North America Puzzle
products.body:
Discover the vibrant birdlife of Eastern North America with this beautifully illustrated 1000-piece puzzle by Bird Collective. Featuring a stunning array of birds—from the striking Red-bellied Woodpecker to the colorful Blue Jay and the elegant Great Blue Heron—this puzzle captures the diversity of the region’s feathered friends. The intricate scene is set in a lush forest, where over 30 species of birds come to life in rich detail. 

Included is an identification key to help identify each bird, making it both fun and educational. Whether you're a dedicated birder or a casual puzzle enthusiast, this engaging and interactive puzzle will provide hours of entertainment and discovery.

products.title: Sunprint Kit
products.body:
Art & science for the curious! Sunprint kits encourage an interest in the photographic process using only sun, water, and a bit of imagination. Place this light-sensitive paper in the sun and you can capture the image of whatever you place on it. Wash with water to make the image permanent. The kit makes a great summer project and a forever-favorite birthday gift and stocking stuffer. 

Each individual packet contains 12 4"x4" sheets and an acrylic overlay.

products.title: Great Blue Heron Patch
products.body:
#64 Great Blue Heron

From the riverbanks to farm fields of North America, these tall, majestic wading birds patiently stalk their prey. Though mostly fish eaters, they won’t turn down frogs, voles, gophers, salamanders, turtles, snakes and birds. That diet allows some individuals to stay up north in the winter, even around frozen waters.

products.body: Featuring a trio of loons surrounded by a burst of colorful, abstract flora, this sticker will add a touch of the otherworldly to just about anything.

products.body: Take your adventures to a higher dimension with our Cosmic Loon tee.

products.title: Cosmic Loons Boxy Tank
products.body: Take your adventures to another dimension with this our Cosmic Loon muscle tank. Featuring the Common Loon, it's anything but common.

products.title: Eastern Towhee Patch
products.body:
#63 Eastern Towhee

These bulky and boldly-patterned sparrows prefer undergrowth habitat and can often be heard scratching away at the leaf litter. In the breeding season, the males usually shed their furtiveness and sing from a conspicuous perch. The females (pictured here) build their cup nests on the ground or close to it in shrubs. Their name comes from one of their most familiar calls: a two-part, rising “towhee.”

products.title: Nocs Pro Issue 8x42 Binoculars
products.body: Nocs Provisions full size binoculars are great for birdwatching. Offering a wide field of view with edge to edge clarity, a Swiss-designed prism, and a close focus lens of 6', these go-to optics provide a rich and color correct image. Fully waterproof and fogproof, you'll be able to bird from dawn to dusk in all weather conditions.

products.title: Ruddy Turnstone Patch
products.body:
#62 Ruddy Turnstone

The chunky, short-legged, calico-patterned Ruddy Turnstone is, like most shorebirds, a long-distance traveler. It breeds in the arctic tundra and winters on rocky shorelines and sandy beaches on six continents. The wet, slippery rocks of those shorelines would be tough for some birds (or us) to navigate, but Ruddy Turnstones have feet adapted to them and a low center of gravity that keeps them grounded.

products.title: Nocs Zoom Tube 8x32 Monocular
products.body: Nocs Provisions ultra compact optical tool ready for any journey. Fully multi-coated optics and a wide field of view bring nature closer, and the rugged, water resistant housing keeps the elements at bay. It's the perfect everyday carry optical tool for those who want a handy and intimate view of nature or their environment.

products.title: Nocs Standard Issue 8x25 Binoculars
products.body: Nocs Provisions compact binoculars put top shelf optics in a compact, lightweight and durable frame. Small enough to tuck into your bag, they're perfect for travel, hiking, and observing wildlife while on the go.

products.body:

Note the special edition Audubon Ruddy Duck colorway comes with a matching woven neck strap. The other colorways come with a thinner black neck strap.

products.title: Roseate Tern Patch
products.body:
#61 Roseate Tern

Roseate Terns are dazzling in their crisp white breeding plumage, a black cap, dark bill, and the pale rosy tint that gives them their name. They were the target of fashion hunters in the late 19th century, and they remain vulnerable to rising sea levels and human development.

products.title: Western Kingbird Patch
products.body:
#60 Western Kingbird

This large flycatcher of open country in the west has adapted well to human development over the last century. Roadside fences and utility lines offer them hunting perches from which they sally out to catch flying insects, while utility poles provide nest sites. And they will aggressively defend those nests from much larger predators like ravens, hawks, and falcons that stray too close. Compared to other yellow-bellied kingbirds, notice their ashy head and the white outer feathers on their black tail.

products.title: Beach Life Hat
products.body: This embroidered hat details all kinds of beach life found in sand, sea and sky. Can you spot the Piping Plover? You'll also see Horseshoe Crabs, Ruddy Turnstones, Red Knot, Striped Bass and flounder.

products.title: Common Yellowthroat Patch
products.body:
#59 Common Yellowthroat

One of the most numerous and widespread warblers, the Common Yellowthroat is loud and, in the case of the black-masked males, unmistakable. It’s the only North American warbler that nests in open marshes, and can be found from coast to coast when breeding. Though often hidden in reeds and thickets, the male will climb up to belt out his distinctive song, wichity-wichity-wichity.

One of its greatest threats, as for all songbirds, are collisions with glass, often as a result of light pollution. So please make your windows feather-friendly and turn off non-essential lights at night.

products.title: Woodpeckers of North America Knit Blanket
products.body: This beautifully knit blanket showcases nine woodpeckers species found in North America in a geometric design.

products.body:

Now you can have a steady stream of colorful visitors year-round, by joining our Birding Patch Club. Every month, we'll send you our newest embroidered patch. Whether it's a familiar friend or a new species you'd like to add to your life list, each one is an emblem of our commitment to live in harmony with nature.

products.body: Woodpeckers are hard to miss, with their contrasting colors and dexterous drumming. This heavyweight tee features 10 of our favorite woodpeckers found in North America.

products.title: Northern Flicker Patch
products.body:
#58 Northern Flicker Patch

While most woodpeckers stick to trees, the Northern Flicker digs for ants and beetles on the ground with its long, slightly curved bill. There are two forms, the Yellow-shafted in the east and Red-shafted in the west, which will interbreed where they overlap. Both have bright pops of color under their wings and tails when they fly. They range from Alaska to Nicaragua, but don’t expect to find them in large unbroken forests; they need at least some open ground to find those ants.

products.title: Common Raven Patch
products.body:
#57 Common Raven Patch

Poe knew: Ravens are passerines: “still is sitting, still is sitting.” The largest in the order of perching birds, or songbirds, their “songs” consist of loud croaks and strange musical notes. Ravens are scavengers and predators, and for centuries have followed human settlement knowing they can find a quick meal. These acrobatic flyers are remarkably adaptable, living across the continent in habitats as diverse as old-growth forests, high Arctic tundra, arid desert and industrial waterfronts. They are among the smartest of all birds, and experiments have demonstrated their insight when solving problems.

products.title: Barn Owl Patch
products.body:
#56 Barn Owl

Though their name suggests the countryside, Barn Owls can be found in any open habitat, urban to rural, where they nest in natural and human-made cavities like church steeples, caves, cliffs, and boxes. Their low-light vision and hearing are incredible; their ability to locate prey by sound is the best of any animal ever tested. These silent nocturnal predators live on every continent except Antarctica.

products.title: American Goshawk Patch
products.body:
#55 American Goshawk

The American Goshawk is a fast and powerful forest hunter, preying on medium-sized birds like grouse and small mammals. They are widespread across northern North America’s conifer and western mountain forests. Roughly every ten years, when their preys’ populations run low, a number of these secretive birds push south of their normal range in the east and into the valleys of the west.

products.title: Osprey Hat
products.body: This embroidered osprey hat is the perfect everyday accessory to keep the sun off your face. It's a classic and easy dad hat.

products.title: Redhead Patch
products.body:
#54 Redhead

Aptly named, breeding male Redheads cut a striking figure. The females and young are a warm brown with the same blue-gray bill as the males. These social ducks gather in the winter by the tens of thousands in the lagoons of Laguna Madre on the Gulf Coast of Texas and Mexico. In the summer, they breed in reedy ponds along the prairie potholes of the Great Plains and West. Females frequently sneak their eggs into the nests of other duck species, in a strategy known as brood parasitism.

products.title: Duck Trio Tee
products.body: Dabbling or diving? Get to know three iconic ducks with this soft tee, featuring the familiar Mallard, the colorful Wood Duck, and the striking Common Goldeneye.

products.title: American Woodcock Patch
products.body:
#53 American Woodcock

This cryptically-patterned shorebird evolved to live in upland habitats, and has collected many nicknames: timberdoodle, bogsucker, night partridge, big-eye, and mudbat. Its large eyes, set high and wide on the sides of its head, allow it to watch for danger from all directions as it probes for earthworms. In spring and summer, their spiraling courtship flights and strange vocalizations are hallmarks of forest clearings in the eastern forests of North America.

products.title: The Feminist Bird Club's Birding for a Better World
products.body:
The Feminist Bird Club's Birding for a Better World: A Guide to Finding Joy and Community in Nature

By Molly Adams and Sydney Anderson

Birding is for everyone. That is the sentiment on which the Feminist Bird Club (FBC) was founded in 2016 and the spirit that is celebrated in this original and timely book. In these pages, Molly Adams, FBC founder, and Sydney Golden Anderson offer readers:

  • A celebration of birding and the outdoors
  • Examples of how inclusive, affirming, and joyful an activity birding can be
  • Awareness of the crucial inclusivity issues facing birding communities today
  • Related ideas for radical inclusivity and how to break down barriers around birding for marginalized communities
  • Information on the ecological challenges facing birds and all life on earth including habitat loss and warming temperatures
  • Actionable steps everyone can take toward environmental justice
  • Journaling prompts throughout to offer moments of self-reflection

The Feminist Bird Club's Birding for a Better World illustrates how anyone can engage in the universally available activity of birding, and support equity and environmental justice at the same time, making an excellent gift or self-purchase for seasoned birders and beginners alike, as well as for nature lovers, social justice activists, and anyone seeking actionable information about accessibility and inclusivity in the bird watching community.

Pages: 160

Size: 5.5 x 8 inches

Illustrations: 90 original illustrations from the Feminist Bird Club community.

products.body: Get to know your North American loons with this comfy tee. It features the five species seen on the continent: Common, Arctic, Yellow-Billed, Pacific, and Red-throated loon.

products.title: Birdpedia
products.body:
Birdpedia: A Brief Compendium of Avian Lore

Christopher W. Leahy

Illustrated by Abby McBride

A captivating A–Z treasury about birds and birding

Birdpedia is an engaging illustrated compendium of bird facts and birding lore. Featuring nearly 200 entries—on topics ranging from plumage and migration to birds in art, literature, and folklore—this enticing collection is brimming with wisdom and wit about all things avian.

Christopher Leahy sheds light on "hawk-watching," "twitching," and other rituals from the sometimes mystifying world of birding that entail a good deal more than their names imply. He explains what kind of bird's nests you can eat, why mocking birds mock, and many other curiosities that have induced otherwise sane people to peer into treetops using outrageously expensive optical equipment. Leahy shares illuminating insights about pioneering ornithologists such as John James Audubon and Florence Bailey, and describes unique bird behaviors such as anting, caching, duetting, and mobbing. He discusses avian fossils, the colloquial naming of birds, the science and history of ornithology, and more. The book's convenient size makes it the perfect traveling companion to take along on your own avian adventures.

With charming illustrations by Abby McBride, Birdpedia is a marvelous mix of fact and fancy that is certain to delight seasoned birders and armchair naturalists alike.

products.title: Atlantic Puffin Patch
products.body:
#52 Atlantic Puffin

With their huge multicolored bills, bright orange feet and teary-eyed visage, Atlantic Puffins have been called clowns of the sea. These members of the auk family spend most of their lives on the open ocean and breed on islands in the North Atlantic. Their population plummeted in the 19th century due to hunting, prompting conservation efforts. A re-introduction program started by National Audubon in the1970s has returned them to former nesting islands off Maine. Still, puffins face grave risks today; in their southernmost colonies, they’re experiencing breeding failures as ocean temperatures rise and fish populations shift.

products.title: American Flamingo Patch
products.body:
#51 American Flamingo

Long-legged, long-necked and downright unmistakable, the American Flamingo flocks in shallow, saline lagoons of the Caribbean and Central and northern South America. They feed on algae and aquatic invertebrates like brine shrimp, and the pigments in their food give them their pink coloration. Until 1900, flamingos from the Bahamas regularly migrated to what is now Florida’s Everglades National Park.

products.title: Retro Loon Sticker
products.body: Introducing our stunning Retro Loon Vinyl Sticker, a perfect blend of nostalgia and vibrant colors. Inspired by the iconic retro aesthetics, this high-quality vinyl sticker showcases a magnificent loon in all its glory.

products.title: Eastern Bluebird Enamel Pin
products.body:
Dazzle anyone and bedazzle anything with this cute Eastern Bluebird enamel pin. Featuring the brilliant blue and warm orange plumage of this beloved backyard bird, this colorful bird pin is perfect for jackets, backpacks, hats, totes, and birding bags.

Members of the thrush family, Eastern Bluebirds were once a less common sight, but their populations have rebounded thanks in large part to nest boxes and “bluebird trails.” Look for them catching insects near the ground or feeding on berries around farms, forest clearings, roadsides, and other semi-open habitats.

This cute enamel bird pin makes a perfect little gift for bird lovers, birders, and bluebird fans.

products.title: Red-winged Blackbird Patch
products.body:
#50 Red-winged Blackbird

Red-winged Blackbirds are one of the most abundant birds in North America. The ringing call of the glossy-black males, who puff up and flare their red-and-yellow shoulder patches, is one of the continent’s harbingers of spring. They claim territory early, just about anywhere with standing water and vegetation, and the streaky-brown females soon follow.

products.title: Sibley Birder's Trivia: A Card Game
products.body:
A game for birders to test their knowledge—with 200 cards offering 400 questions of varying difficulty about the birds of North America from the bestselling author and ornithologist David Allen Sibley.

True or false: Many dinosaurs (the ancestors of modern birds) had feathers.

If you answered "true," you just won a point playing this ultimate ornithology trivia game. Sibley Birder's Trivia offers 400 questions that will test your bird knowledge over five rich categories: Bird Identification, Bird Anatomy and Physiology, Bird Names, Bird Behavior, and Birds in Culture. The types of question vary: Q&A, true or false, and multiple choice. Each card offers two questions in a category, one easier and one harder. Players can choose which one they want to answer; the easy question is worth one point, while the hard one is worth two. If you answer the easier one correctly, you can move on to the harder one. 

Some of the questions about identification are illustrated with Sibley's vibrant bird portraits drawn from his authoritative work, The Sibley Guide to Birds, Second Edition. You can play in teams, one-on one, or alone by pulling random cards to test your knowledge. No matter how you play, in the end, everybody wins as they learn hundreds of fascinating facts about birds.

products.title: Red Knot Patch
products.body:
#49 Red Knot

The Red Knot gets its name for its rich summer plumage. Salmon-colored from face to belly, this plump, medium-sized sandpiper feeds on horseshoe crab eggs on its journey north, flying approximately 16,000 miles annually between Tierra del Fuego and the Arctic Circle. Red Knots face grave threats, from the overharvesting of horseshoe crabs to coastal development and climate change.

products.title: Cerulean Warbler Patch
products.body:
#48 Cerulean Warbler

If you’re looking for a Cerulean Warbler, brace yourself for warbler neck because these songbirds usually stick to the upper canopy. In the spring, the male’s namesake blue shows on head, back and breastband, while the female is a unique blue-green. Their population has suffered steep declines due to habitat loss, both in the Andes where they spend winters, and in the mature deciduous forests of the eastern U.S. where they breed.

products.title: Black-capped Chickadee Patch
products.body:
#47 Black-capped Chickadee

Bold, social, and lively, the crisply patterned Black-capped Chickadee is a familiar and popular sight in the northern U.S. and Canada, from woodlands to backyard feeders. In winter, chickadees are often the vocal sentinels of mixed flocks of nuthatches, titmice, kinglets and the like. They are largely sedentary, though they make seasonal movements away from their nesting territory during food shortages.

products.title: The Backyard Birdwatcher’s Bible
products.body:
Birds, Behaviors, Habitats, Identification, Art & Other Home Crafts

Paul Sterry, Christopher Perrins, Sonya Patel Ellis, Dominic Couzens

An informative and eye-catching reference book for beginner and intermediate backyard bird enthusiasts. 

The Backyard Birdwatcher’s Bible is that rare type of book, one that is as packed with information as it is pleasing to look at. The latest in a successful line of “bibles,” following The Beekeeper’s Bible and The Botanical Bible, this new volume has the broadest appeal yet. An elegant aesthetic is paired with practical tips on identifying, attracting, and caring for backyard birds, as well as crafting bird-friendly gardens and bird houses. With additional sections focused on everything from the bird life cycle to bird behavior, symbolism, and meaning in art, this authoritative book is brimming with engaging answers to all of your birdwatching questions.

416 Pages, 7.5 x 9.5

Full color photographs and illustrations.

products.title: Saw-whet Owl Enamel Pin
products.body:
Though these fluffy and large-headed owls don’t weigh much more than a robin, they are fierce hunters of small mammals. Saw-whet Owls are found in forests from Alaska to Maine, with some staying year-round and others migrating south in the winter. They can be hard to see due to their secretive and nocturnal habits, but their low, whistled toots carry through the dark wilderness.

products.title: Tufted Titmouse Patch
products.body:
#46 Tufted Titmouse

The slightly comic features of the small, gray, and energetic Tufted Titmouse are enough to warm even the coldest hearts. Its large black eyes and crest like a dorsal fin stand out, as does its voice: a loud, low peter-peter-peter that echoes through the eastern woods it calls home. Tufted titmice are in the same family as chickadees and are similarly loyal visitors to backyard feeders in suburban and urban homes.

products.title: Red-faced Warbler Patch
products.body:
#45 Red-faced Warbler

This sweet singer's bright red sets it apart from all other North American warblers save for the Painted Redstart. The bird’s primary home is in Mexico, but it also breeds in New Mexico's and Arizona's high-elevation conifer forests. Unlike most warblers, the males and females are both brightly colored, and they keep these colors year-round, molting only once.

products.title: Greater Roadrunner Patch
products.body:
#44 Greater Roadrunner

The Greater Roadrunner, a member of the cuckoo family, is an icon of the Southwest. Roadrunners thrive in harsh landscapes, hunting moisture-rich prey like mammals and reptiles to compensate for the scarcity of water in their diet. They’ll even kill and eat rattlesnakes, working in pairs to launch surprise attacks.

products.title: Hawks In Flight Bandana
products.body: Get on the move with this spirited bandana, featuring a series of soaring buteos, accipiters, falcons, and other raptors.

products.title: Yellow-billed Cuckoo Patch
products.body:
#43 Yellow-billed Cuckoo

Long-tailed and furtive, these voracious caterpillar eaters are more commonly heard than seen. Legend has it that they call before thunderstorms, a trait that earned them the nickname “rain crow.” The western U.S. breeding population has largely disappeared due to the devastation of their native riparian habitats and is listed as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act.

products.title: Sibley Backyard Birds Matching Game
products.body:
Featuring beautiful watercolor bird illustrations from leading ornithologist David Sibley, this 40-piece matching game is sure to charm both children and parents.

The Sibley Backyard Birds Matching Game works your memory with 40 pieces, featuring 20 backyard birds, including blue jays, sparrows, and hummingbirds. The beautiful hand-painted illustrations are designed to grab the attention of kids and parents alike.

products.title: Scott's Oriole Patch
products.body:
#42 Scott's Oriole

Boldly colored and vocal, Scott’s Orioles inhabit the high deserts and adjoining mountain slopes of the arid Southwest. They begin singing before sunrise and continue through the sun-parched hours of the day. Scott’s Orioles have a special relationship with yucca plants, where they forage for insects and nectar, and weave nests out of and amidst their leaves.

products.title: Caspian Tern Patch
products.body:
#41 Caspian Tern

The Caspian is the world’s largest tern. Though named for the Caspian Sea, where early ornithologists first observed it, this fish-hunter with a massive red bill ranges across five continents. In North America, Caspians largely nest on inland lakes and rivers; the world’s largest known colony, with more than 6,000 breeding pairs each year, occupies a small, artificial island in the Columbia River between Oregon and Washington.

products.title: Ruby-throated Hummingbird Patch
products.body:
#40 Ruby-throated Hummingbird

Bold and brilliant, Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are eastern North America’s only breeding hummingbird, a dazzling sight of red and green as they buzz around flower gardens or backyard feeders in search of nectar. These tiny birds will migrate across the Gulf of Mexico in a single flight, beating their wings about 53 times a second. Most spend winters in Central America.

products.title: Northern Cardinal Enamel Pin
products.body:
The Northern Cardinal's bold colors and clear song enlivens wintery and warm days alike. Keep this wide-ranging and striking bird close to your heart with this shiny silver enamel pin.

1.25" wide x 1.3" tall

Shiny silver hard enamel pin with black rubber clutch backing attachment.

This pin is celebrates Alabama Audubon’s conservation work in one of America’s most biodiverse states.

products.title: Blue-winged Teal Patch
products.body:
#39 Blue-winged Teal

Small dabbling ducks, Blue-winged Teals migrate relatively late in spring and early in fall, and most spend winters outside the United States, some as far as South America. They nest on the ground near ponds and marshes, and young Blue-wings are forced to mature quickly: they leave the nest within 24 hours after hatching.

products.title: Black-necked Stilt Patch
products.body:
#38 Black-necked Stilt

Delicate looking shorebirds with long pink legs, Black-necked Stilts forage in shallow wetlands, walking purposefully in search of tiny invertebrates. Their range spans from Argentina all the way to the Pacific Northwest, and there’s also a Hawaiian subspecies. They belong to the same family as the American Avocet, another elegant black-and-white shorebird.

products.title: Prothonotary Warbler Patch
products.body:
#37 Prothonotary Warbler

A golden songbird of wooded swamps and lowland forests, the Prothonotary Warbler is said to be named for a group of Catholic clerks who wore bright yellow robes. Unlike other eastern warblers, it nests in tree cavities and will even take birdhouses placed near water. With their beady eyes and blue-gray wings, even the dullest individuals are still a brilliant, unmistakable yellow.

products.title: Common Loon Camp Hat
products.body: Timeless as a loon on a summer lake, our loon camp hat is the perfect companion for your outdoor adventures.

products.title: American Goldfinch Patch
products.body:
#36 American Goldfinch

Bright and chatty, the American Goldfinch enlivens meadows, weedy roadsides, forest edges and bird feeders across the country. In summertime the males are a brilliant yellow and black, and in the winter, males and females turn a duller brown and gather at feeders. They eat seeds primarily from the daisy family, and nest in the late summer, timed with the peak crop of these flowering plants.

products.title: Backyard Birds Bumper Sticker
products.body: Support your local birds with this bright and cheery bumper sticker.

products.title: Northern Cardinal Patch
products.body:
#35 Northern Cardinal

The official bird of no fewer than seven eastern states, the Northern Cardinal has led countless people to open a field guide or pick up binoculars for the first time. Cardinals have been extending their range northward for decades, in part, it seems, due to the spread of feeders filled with sunflower seeds. The vivid red male brightens any snowy day, and both males and females sing in the spring.

products.title: Northern Pygmy-Owl Patch
products.body:
#34 Northern Pygmy-Owl

Small, stealthy and ferocious, Northern Pygmy-Owls live year-round in the mountains of western North America and hunt by day. Though not much larger than sparrows, they’ll catch prey up to three times their size. They’re hard to spot, but small birds making a ruckus in the vicinity of one can tip off their presence.

products.title: Hawks in Flight Nalgene Water Bottle | Seafoam
products.body: This water bottle will help you stay on your toes with your buteos and answer that recurring question....Sharpie or Cooper's? It catalogs a roster of raptors in flight. Now every day can be a hawk watch day!

products.title: Chickadee Corduroy Hat
products.body:
Celebrate your love for birds with the Chickadee Corduroy Hat from Bird Collective. Designed for everyday wear, this classic cap blends comfort, durability, and bird-inspired style.

Made from 100% cotton corduroy, the hat has a soft texture with a sturdy feel that holds up to regular use. It’s easy to wear whether you’re birding at dawn, heading out for a walk, or running errands around town.

An embroidered chickadee sits front and center as a tribute to one of North America’s most beloved backyard birds. The unstructured six-panel crown creates a relaxed look, while the flat bill adds a timeless silhouette. An adjustable fabric strap with a metal clasp ensures a comfortable, customizable fit for most head sizes.

Versatile and easy to style, this corduroy hat pairs well with outdoor gear and everyday outfits alike. Wear it year-round or gift it to a fellow bird lover — it’s a go-to accessory built for both function and personality.

products.title: California Quail Patch
products.body:
#29 California Quail

California Quails are richly-patterned, round birds that can be found hurrying across clearings in brushy areas of California and the Northwest. Their most distinctive feature is their comma-shaped head plume, which is actually a cluster of six overlapping feathers. California's state bird, they avoid mountains and stick to the coast and valleys.

products.title: Boat-tailed Grackle Patch
products.body:
#27 Boat-tailed Grackle

This glossy blackbird is a fixture of the Gulf and Atlantic coasts, from saltwater marshes to beachside restaurants where it scavenges for leftovers. Until the 1970s, the Boat-tailed Grackle was considered to be the same species as the Great-tailed Grackle, with which it overlaps in Texas and Louisiana, but its coastal range has moved northward following human development.

products.title: Belted Kingfisher Patch
products.body:
#25 Belted Kingfisher 

The rattling call of the blue-gray Belted Kingfisher heralds its presence along rivers and shorelines as it plunges for fish and other aquatic prey. Big-headed, stocky, and heavy-billed, this kingfisher nests in earthen burrows and is widespread throughout North America. The female is particularly striking with its rust-orange belly band.

products.title: Brown Pelican Patch
products.body:
#23 Brown Pelican

An unmistakable bird of southern coasts, Brown Pelicans glide low over the surf in single file and plunge-dive for small fish with their gigantic bills. As recently as the 1970s they were nearly endangered, but conservationists brought them back from the brink by pushing for bans on DDT and other harmful pesticides.

products.title: Cedar Waxwing Patch
products.body:
#20 Cedar Waxwing

In fall and winter, squadrons of Cedar Waxwings roam widely in search of fruiting trees. They look like sleek superheroes, with black masks, shiny suits, and dabs of red and yellow on their wings and tails. In summer they eat insects but the rest of the year berries, making them one of the few species in North America that specializes in eating fruit.

products.title: Canyon Wren Patch
products.body:
#19 Canyon Wren

From cliff faces or steep canyon walls, this skulky, rust-colored, pot-bellied wren is much easier heard than seen. Its cascading, liquid song echoes out of those crags, where it probes for prey with its thin bill. Males like to sing from rocky perches in the spring and summer, though, so with patience they can be viewed well.

products.title: Evening Grosbeak Patch
products.body:
#18 Evening Grosbeak

These stocky, big-billed finches range widely in winter, traveling in colorful flocks and frequently crashing bird feeders and consuming large amounts of sunflower seeds. Once seen only in the West, in the last century they’ve expanded their range eastward with the addition of new food sources.

products.title: Common Loon Patch
products.body:
#17 Common Loon

The Common Loon – a "veritable avian submarine" as the American Bird Conservancy puts it – are incredible swimmers and divers, and their eerie, mournful wails are the soundtrack of wilderness summer nights in northern forests. They're also unforgettable sights on woodland lakes in the breeding season, with a red eye, white necklace and black-and-white checkerboard back.

products.title: California Condor Patch
products.body:
#14 California Condor

Behold the California Condor, North America’s largest land bird! The condor became extinct in the wild in the late ‘80s, with the remaining individuals brought into captivity. An ambitious and historic conservation and reintroduction campaign has brought the wild population back up to almost 500 - so there’s much work to still be done.

products.title: Black-throated Sparrow Patch
products.body:
#12 Black-throated Sparrow

A resident of arid lands, the neatly-patterned Black-throated Sparrow certainly lives up to its name. But despite its bold throat, its sand-gray and brown body helps it blend in with its desert habitats. Listen for their quiet tinkling calls as they forage on the ground among creosote bushes and cacti.

products.title: Bobolink Patch
products.body:
#6 Bobolink

The bubbling, R2D2-like song of the male Bobolink flutters out of hayfields and meadows in the spring and summer. In the fall, the male sheds its tuxedoed appearance and wears the striped brown plumage of the female. Heading south in migration, they will often stop to feed in rice fields.

products.title: American Kestrel Patch
products.body:
#2 American Kestrel

North America’s smallest and most widespread falcon, the American Kestrel can be found perched on roadside fences as well as on rooftops in the densest cities. For their size, they’re fearsome predators, and their shrill call often announces their presence. They hunt by rapidly beating their wings to hover in place, scanning open territory below for grasshoppers or other small prey.

products.title: Eastern Bluebird Patch
products.body:
#8 Eastern Bluebird

Members of the thrush family, Eastern Bluebirds were once a more uncommon sight, but their numbers have increased recently owing in large part to birdhouses put up for them, especially along “bluebird trails.” You can find them catching insects near the ground or feeding on berries by farms, forest clearings, roadsides, and other semi-open habitats.

products.title: Black Skimmer Patch
products.body:
#10 Black Skimmer

The unmistakable Black Skimmer gets its name from its unique manner of feeding. They fly low over waves, with their longer lower mandible knifing through the water and snapping shut once it finds a fish. They’re agile flyers, and in groups often turn and glide in harmony.

Skimmers lay their eggs directly on the beach, which makes them vulnerable to human disturbance, predation, and weather. In New York State, where only three nesting colonies remain, NYC Audubon is working with city and state agencies to protect their breeding habitat  and band chicks every summer.

products.body:

You are bird enthusiasts—researchers, bird watchers, ornithologists, and collectors—seeking to discover and attract the best birds to your network of wildlife preserves. products.title: Northern Harrier Patch
products.body:
#33 Northern Harrier

Unique among North American hawks, the Northern Harrier favors marshes and grasslands where it glides low with long V-shaped wings in search of small mammals and birds. Its owl-like face, unhurried flight style, and white rump are telltale field marks. Females are brown and larger than the gray-and-white males.

products.title: House Finch Enamel Pin
products.body:
Brighten up anything with this fun and friendly House Finch pin!

Social and gregarious, House Finches are widespread across the continent, from suburban yards to mountain slopes. Once exclusive to the Western U.S. and Mexico, a small number were introduced to New York in 1940 and they’ve since spread across the country. The males sing a lively, warbling song, and the red of their head and breast are a welcome sight at any feeder. 

1.25" wide x 1.25" tall

This design is inspired by the Finch Research Network (FiRN), a non-profit that works to grow our understanding of finches.

products.title: Golden Eagle Patch
products.body:
#32 Golden Eagle

Revered, fearsome raptors, Golden Eagles hunt for jackrabbits and other small mammals in North America’s wild, open country, particularly in the West. Their golden nape is a signature field mark. These large, dark-brown birds occupy an important place in many Indigenous cultures in North America, and they’re also found in Europe and Asia.

This patch celebrates HawkWatch International, a non-profit that monitors and safeguards the long-term health of this special bird.

products.title: Purple Gallinule Patch
products.body:
#31 Purple Gallinule

One of North America’s most colorful birds, the Purple Gallinule is the star of any freshwater marsh, where it steps across water lilies with its long yellow legs and toes in search of invertebrates. A year-round resident of wetlands from Florida to Central America, this bird also breeds in a handful of southeastern U.S. states. Vagrants have turned up from Iceland to South Africa.

products.title: I'm With The Birds Sticker
products.body: This fun sticker features some of our favorite birds and will let everyone know you're on their side.

products.title: Snowy Plover Patch
products.body:
#30 Snowy Plover

Easy to miss but hard to forget, the tiny sand-colored Snowy Plover perfectly blends into its surroundings, such as Pacific Coast beaches and interior salt flats. They forage in a stop-start manner higher up the beach rather than by the water’s edge, and for their nests they make shallow scrapes in the ground. Young Snowy Plovers leave the nest within 3 hours of hatching and begin foraging on their own almost immediately.

products.title: Osprey Patch
products.body:
#28 Osprey

Supreme anglers, Ospreys are found on every continent except for Antarctica. These rangy hawks hunt for fish with long, hooked talons, their yellow eyes studying the water below. In North America, their numbers have recovered dramatically since the ban on the pesticide DDT. They often build their nests on man-made platforms and other artificial structures, returning to them year after year.

products.title: Steller's Jay Patch
products.body:
#26 Steller's Jay

Vocal residents of the western U.S., Steller’s Jays are regularly found in conifer forests, wooded campgrounds, and backyards. Outside of nesting season they travel in flocks, with their harsh, scolding calls signaling their arrival. These inquisitive birds aren’t shy with humans, and patrol feeders and campsites looking for handouts.

products.title: Red-headed Woodpecker Patch
products.body:
#24 Red-headed Woodpecker

Sometimes called a “flying checkerboard,” the Red-headed Woodpecker is a stunning but infrequent sight in eastern North America, where its open-country habitat has declined. It’s the only North American woodpecker that stores and then covers its food, like insects or acorns, underneath bark.

products.title: Green Heron Patch
products.body:
#22 Green Heron

The stocky and secretive Green Heron is a solitary hunter of small fish in dense marshes, ponds, and wooded riverbanks. A richly colored bird of chestnut and iridescent green, the Green Heron often raises and lowers its crest as it waits patiently for prey, and will sometimes drop “bait,” like a feather or twig, on the water’s surface to lure it in.

products.title: Swallow-tailed Kite Patch
products.body:
#21 Swallow-tailed Kite

These graceful, buoyant black-and-white birds of prey are summer visitors to cypress swamps and open pine woods in the Southeast, where they raise their young before migrating to South America. A joy to watch, Swallow-tailed Kites use their deeply-forked tail to twist, swoop and glide in the sky, catching small animals and insects on the wing.

products.title: Retro Common Loon Lightweight Tee
products.body: Feeling nostalgic for those long summer evenings where the wail of the Common Loon felt like the call of the wild? Wrap yourself up in those good old days with this classic and comfy tee.

products.title: Kirtland's Warbler Patch
products.body:
#16 Kirtland’s Warbler

This steel blue and yellow songbird was covered by the original Endangered Species Act, and in the 1980s there were fewer than 200 breeding pairs left in the world. Kirtland's Warblers breed in young jack pine forests, almost exclusively in the Lower Peninsula of Michigan, and with decades-long efforts by federal, state and nonprofit agencies, they've made a comeback to more than 2,000 pairs. Proceeds from this patch will support the American Bird Conservancy as it works to expand its habitat, both in the U.S. and its wintering sites in The Bahamas, and plan for its future off the Endangered Species list.

products.title: Golden-winged Warbler Patch
products.body:
#15 Golden-Winged Warbler

The Golden-winged Warbler has lost about two-thirds of its population, and today roughly 400,000 breeding pairs remain. But in the northern forests of the Great Lakes, where about 90 percent of the world's population nest every spring and summer, the American Bird Conservancy is working to restore their preferred habitat. Proceeds from this patch will support ABC's on-the-ground efforts to keep the Golden-winged Warbler from becoming endangered.

products.title: King Eider Patch
products.body:
#13 King Eider

The male King Eider is one of the most strikingly-patterned ducks in the world. King Eiders breed in the high Arctic in summer, and spend their winters on open ocean, mostly at the edge of sea ice or off rocky coasts, occasionally as far south as the Mid-Atlantic states. Their spring migration past northern Alaska is an incredible phenomenon: 360,000 King Eiders were once counted in 10 hours.

products.title: Short-eared Owl Patch
products.body:
#7 Short-eared Owl

Birders never forget the sight of a “shortie” hunting over grasslands at dusk. Their long, broad wings beat with a mothlike quality in flight. Their tiny ear tufts are difficult to see – but not the bird itself (if you know where to look), since it’s one of the few owl species that hunts during daylight.

products.title: Scarlet Tanager Patch
products.body:
#9 Scarlet Tanager

Who can forget the first time they saw a Scarlet Tanager? Breeding males are a brilliant red with black wings and tails, and females wear hues of olive-yellow. They look exotic in the eastern forests where they breed, and they spend their non-breeding months in tropical rainforests of the Andes lowlands, when both males and females are a more muted yellow-green.

products.title: Red-breasted Nuthatch Patch
products.body:
#5 Red-breasted Nuthatch

This charming little songbird loves conifers, and will work its way up and down a spruce or pine looking for insects and seeds. They’re hardly shy, though, and unafraid to come close to humans – they might even grab food off your hand on a cold winter day. And although they’re typically found up north, they’ll head south when cone crops fail in their boreal forests.

products.title: Loggerhead Shrike Patch
products.body:
#11 Loggerhead Shrike

The “Butcherbird,” as the masked Loggerhead Shrike is known, is a songbird that acts like a raptor. In grasslands and open country, it preys on insects, birds, lizards, and small mammals, and because it lacks a raptor’s talons, it skewers its kill on thorns or barbed wire. Although their numbers have dropped sharply in North America, they’re still quite common in the South and regularly perch on fence posts and power lines.

products.title: Northern Parula Patch
products.body:
#1 Northern Parula

One of the smallest wood-warblers, the bluish-gray Northern Parula breeds in the eastern half of North America, from Florida to the boreal forest, building nests out of moss. The breeding males, with their chestnut bands on yellow chests, are lively singers during spring migration, which helps locate them in the upper forest canopy.

products.title: Pileated Woodpecker Patch
products.body:
#3 Pileated Woodpecker 

The Pileated Woodpecker, with its flame-red crest and black-and-white body, is an electrifying sight in eastern and mountain-west forests. Their numbers have slowly rebounded as those forests regrew after widespread clearing in the 18th and 19th centuries. You can find them banging away at dead wood in search of carpenter ants, their main prey, and the unique rectangular holes they leave behind are used for shelter by other birds.

products.title: Hooded Merganser Patch
products.body:
#4 Hooded Merganser

These small ducks with yellow eyes light up winter birding on freshwater ponds and protected saltwater bays. The males fan their distinctive black-and-white crests while courting the cinnamon-brown females. In the summer they nest in tree cavities, and their ducklings depart the nest by jumping all the way down to the ground within 24 hours of hatching.
